name: Septal extension graft

lead: A septal extension graft attaches cartilage to the end of the septum in rhinoplasty so the surgeon can set the tip's position, length, projection and rotation. It is used mostly for weak or underprojected tips, and in looksmaxxing discussion it is associated with lengthening or rotating the nose tip.

A general reference says it gives more control and changes less over time than a columellar strut; a 2019 cohort compared the two. The evidence is case series, comparative cohorts and several registered trials.

paras: Cartilage, usually harvested from the septum, is fixed to the caudal septum, creating a stable platform for the tip cartilages. The new tip position shows after swelling settles.

A 2014 study reported complications of the graft in Asian patients, and trials against columellar struts are ongoing. As with other rhinoplasty, revision surgery can be needed. It is performed by surgeons under anaesthesia.

angle.text: A septal extension graft sets the nose tip's position, projection and rotation in rhinoplasty, especially when the lower lateral cartilages are weak. Cartilage extends the septum to give a stable platform for the tip, and the change is visible after healing. It is an established technique with growing comparative data.

lead: A septal extension graft is a piece of cartilage, usually from the septum, attached to the end of the nasal septum in rhinoplasty to control the position, length, projection and rotation of the nasal tip. It is used particularly in patients with weak lower lateral cartilages.[1][2]
In looksmaxxing discussion it is associated with lengthening or rotating the nose tip. The evidence is surgical case series, comparative cohort studies and several registered trials.
infobox: 1997 paper in Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery

paras: A 1997 paper identified methods for controlling nasal tip position and shape in patients at risk of losing projection, whose noses showed a weak midvault, a plunging tip with a "Polly beak" and drawn-up alae, and reported on septal extension grafts.[1] A 2014 introduction in Archives of Plastic Surgery describes the graft,[3] and a 2007 paper describes a complete septal extension graft for Korean patients using an extensive harvesting technique.[4]
Wikipedia's rhinoplasty article says the septal extension graft gives more tip control and changes less over time than a columellar strut.[2]

A 2014 JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery study reported complications of septal extension grafts in Asian patients.[5] Reviews of Asian rhinoplasty note that cartilage grafts carry a risk of revision surgery from issues such as warping.[6]

A 2019 retrospective cohort compared maintenance of tip projection and rotation after columellar strut versus caudal septal extension graft, noting that no quantitative comparison existed beforehand.[7] Registered trials include comparisons of septal extension graft versus columellar strut (NCT06958575),[8] unilateral versus bilateral grafts in droopy tips (NCT07446426)[9] and a patient-reported outcomes study (NCT07531810).[10]

timeline.event: Septal extension grafts are described as a method of controlling tip projection and shape.[1]
A quantitative comparison of columellar strut and septal extension graft is published.[7]
